My take is that restaurants are dealing with a difficult combination of thin margins, uneven demand and really unforgiving operations. A restaurant can look busy on paper and still have a difficult night if everyone arrives at once, a section is understaffed or the tables aren't turning as expected.

So I wouldn't assume the industry's biggest technology need is simply more reservations. It's helping operators turn demand into a service they can deliver well and profitably.

That makes OpenTable interesting because it sits between the diner looking for a table and the restaurant deciding what it can actually accommodate. My working hypothesis is that the next wave of value comes from better availability, pacing and revenue decisions, with much less manual work at the host stand.

I'd want to validate which part of that problem is most painful by restaurant segment. A fine-dining venue and a busy neighborhood restaurant may have very different constraints.

questions.answer:
I'd put three problems at the top. One is profitability: costs move, demand changes, but restaurants don't have unlimited room to raise prices. The second is uncertainty: a full reservation book doesn't guarantee everyone shows up, and a quiet Tuesday isn't fixed by having a great Saturday.

The third is service capacity. A dining room has physical tables, but its usable capacity also depends on servers, kitchen throughput, party mix and how long guests stay.

Those problems interact. If I push more bookings into a service that's already stretched, I might raise covers and lower the quality of the meal. So before choosing a feature, I'd ask where a specific restaurant is losing money or time, and whether OpenTable can actually change that outcome.

I'm not suggesting building another basic table automation — OpenTable already has those. I'd test whether more contextual recommendations or better execution of the existing tools produces measurable incremental seated value.

I would put direct labor scheduling or dynamic menu pricing behind that for now. They're important problems, but less obviously owned by this product surface and potentially more disruptive to restaurant workflows. OpenTable's advantage, to me, is the connection between demand and the restaurant's actual book. It can see the diner trying to find a table, and it gives operators tools to decide when and how that table should be available.

That matters because a recommendation only creates value if somebody can act on it. A general analytics provider might forecast demand, but a restaurant still needs to translate that forecast into pacing, inventory or guest communication.

I'd look at ways of closing that loop: show the opportunity, recommend a specific action, make it easy to approve or override, then measure whether it helped. That's a more defensible position than simply saying OpenTable has a lot of data.

I see the strongest opportunity in decisions that happen repeatedly under uncertainty. How much demand will we see in the next two hours? Is this table likely to be free in time? Does opening another seating slot help, or will it overwhelm the floor?

Predictive models could be useful when those decisions depend on lots of interacting signals, but I would start with the action. If the forecast says a Friday service is running behind, can the product recommend a pacing change the host can actually use?

The operator should understand the reason and retain control. I'd test whether the recommendation reduces avoidable empty capacity or late seating without adding guest complaints or staff overload. The model is useful only when the better prediction leads to a better service.

I'd also question complex predictive models where a clear rules-based workflow already solves most of the problem. OpenTable's table automations are a good example of existing capability we should benchmark against, not reinvent.

My test would be straightforward: which decision gets better, by how much, and is that improvement worth the complexity and risk?

There's a revenue-management argument for it, but restaurants aren't airlines. Price changes can feel personal, affect the guest relationship and create front-of-house confusion. It also isn't the first place I'd expect OpenTable's existing reservation and table-management data to give us a clear advantage.

I'd rather prove value with more controllable decisions: availability, cancellation recovery and helpful pacing recommendations that operators can approve. Those can build trust without asking restaurants to change how guests perceive their hospitality.

I'd revisit pricing in an environment where variability is already expected, like special experiences or events, if customers and operators actually want it. The question isn't whether we can optimize something — it's whether we should.

I'd define the outcome as incremental seated revenue or contribution, where we have enough cost data. Then I'd choose an experiment that can detect displacement — for example, a randomized restaurant-level or market-level rollout, depending on whether diners can substitute between nearby venues.

questions.answer:
Top five restaurant problems, in my working priority order:

1. Profitable use of limited service capacity. Even when tables exist, staffing, kitchen throughput, party mix and timing decide what the room can handle. OpenTable relevance: availability, pacing, turn times. Test whether better recommendations convert usable idle capacity into seated value.

2. Demand volatility and missed visits. Late cancellations, no-shows and weak weekday periods can leave otherwise usable capacity empty. OpenTable relevance: demand discovery, guest communications, waitlists. Test net recovered contribution, not no-show percentage in isolation.

3. Thin margins and costs that bookings don't reveal. More covers might require costly promotions or overtime. OpenTable relevance: commercial reporting and POS integrations where available. Distinguish revenue, contribution and attribution.

4. Front-of-house operating load. Hosts need fast, trustworthy decisions during live service; wrong information creates seating conflicts and guest frustration. OpenTable relevance: existing one-tap controls and automation. Explore operator-approved prediction, not duplicating controls.

5. International workflow fragmentation. A translated interface doesn't solve differences in reservation culture, deposits, POS, payments, local integrations and service style. OpenTable relevance: configurable core platform with market-specific extensions.

Ranking is a strategic hypothesis, not verified OpenTable customer research. Validate with operators, product/retention data and market-level evidence. I would initially prioritize capacity-aware, operator-controlled decision support; then cancellation recovery and demand shaping; then broader AI and market-specific extensions.

Existing publicly documented capabilities include Table Automations, Turn Times and Availability Insights, Guest Relationship Management, and conversational reporting in testing. Do not pitch these foundational features as new inventions.

questions.answer:
I'd change the deposit rollout rather than declare victory on the no-show rate. We're probably making some diners more reliable while discouraging others from booking at all.

First I'd look at the net number of seated covers and the contribution of those visits, not just the percentage of reservations that show up. Then I'd break it down by first-time versus repeat diner, booking lead time, restaurant type and risk of a no-show.

My likely move would be to keep deposits where the cost of a missed table is genuinely high — perhaps a large party or a scarce experience — and reduce friction elsewhere. I'd test that against the current policy, watching conversion, actual seated revenue and complaints.

If regulation ruled deposits out for certain bookings, I'd remove them for those bookings. I wouldn't try to disguise the same restriction as another payment step. We'd test permitted options like clearer confirmations and waitlist recovery instead.

I'd slow or pause the aggressive pacing change for affected restaurants. More covers are only a win if the staff can deliver the service and people want to come back.

I'd check where experience scores fell — was it particular restaurants, service windows or table types? Then I'd sit with hosts and servers. Are guests actually being rushed, are parties waiting even longer, or is the kitchen receiving too many orders at once?

I'd separate different interventions. More accurate turn-time estimates might help, while shortening every table duration might not. I'd test a narrower recommendation with operator control, and use seating delays, complaints, staff overrides and repeat visits as guardrails alongside incremental covers.

If key partners wanted the feature off, I'd give them that control while we diagnosed it. We shouldn't make the floor harder to run to protect a revenue metric.

I'd stop calling it a success. A 15% booking lift with flat profitability suggests we're shifting demand, attracting lower-value visits or adding costs that offset the revenue.

I'd trace it from booked reservations through actual seated parties, average check, promotions, incremental labor and service mix. For example, an early-dinner campaign might pull guests from a later full-price seating instead of bringing in new visits.

If the problem is concentrated in discounted peak-hour bookings, I'd stop expanding that treatment and test more targeted off-peak demand instead. If there's no path to incremental contribution, I'd end the experiment.

I'd rather report that we learned what *didn't* work than keep investing because the reservations chart looks good.

I'd watch real services and ask why recommendations aren't used. Are they arriving at the wrong time? Are they asking a manager to make changes the floor can't handle? Is the reasoning unclear? Or do operators simply not believe the commercial claim?

I'd agree that the outcome comes first. If operators need near-term revenue and we have a modest extension of existing workflows that can deliver it, I wouldn't force a brand-new AI system onto the roadmap simply because the company is AI-first.

I'd compare the options on likely impact, delivery time, confidence and dependency risk. For example, making the existing cancellation-recovery workflow easier to use might be a better first release than an ambitious new forecasting model.

That doesn't mean abandoning AI. I'd preserve a small validation track if we can afford it — maybe an offline model benchmark or manual recommendations — so we learn whether prediction meaningfully beats the rules baseline.

If we truly only have capacity for one initiative, I'd choose one and explain what evidence would change that call. Half-funding both would be worse.

I'd look at three points in the journey: before booking, between booking and arrival, and during the service itself.

Before booking, diners may see no availability even when the restaurant could accept a different party size or time. After booking, late cancellations and no-shows can leave tables empty. During service, unexpected delays or staffing changes can make the published inventory inaccurate.

I think the most interesting opportunity is connecting those moments. For example, if an early cancellation occurs, can we tell whether it can be filled without overwhelming the kitchen, then match it to real nearby demand?

Some underlying tools already exist at OpenTable, so I'd investigate where there is still friction or unused capacity. The priority wouldn't be the point with the largest booking count; it would be where an intervention generates genuine incremental value.

I think of the reservation journey as a chain of promises. A diner searches, finds availability, selects a time and experience, and receives a confirmation. The restaurant needs that booking to appear correctly in the book, reflect the right party size and any special requirements, and be workable against the floor plan.

Closer to service, the restaurant may confirm, change pacing, handle a cancellation or fill a released slot. Then guests arrive, check in, wait or get seated; the host updates table status while servers and the kitchen manage the actual meal. Afterward, there's the guest record, potential feedback and a future visit.

The key is that the reservation isn't the outcome. The outcome is a guest who arrives, gets a good experience and creates value for the restaurant — without leaving staff to reconcile broken information across systems.

questions.answer:
At RBC, one of the products I led was enabling cashback withdrawals for Avion members who weren't RBC banking customers.

The shopping and earning capability already existed, and RBC customers could receive cashback through their deposit accounts. But non-RBC members didn't have that option. As we opened Avion to a broader audience, we needed a way for people to get the money they'd earned without opening an RBC bank account.

We used Interac e-Transfer through an existing enterprise payments capability rather than building a separate payout service. I owned the consumer experience and requirements, working across engineering, enterprise payments, AML, Risk, and Financial Operations.

There were quite a few details behind what looked like a simple withdrawal button: eligibility, available cashback balances and limits, how to distinguish a submitted request from a completed payment, what happened if a transfer failed or expired, and how the cashback records reconciled to actual payouts. We also needed clear expectations about timing.

The capability supported about 3,200 requests per quarter, roughly 99% processed within 24 hours, and about $1.2 million in annualized payouts. The broader payments service supported over five million annual settlement events, but that wasn't the volume of this feature.

The lesson was that shipping a payment experience isn't just exposing an endpoint. The product only works if the customer journey, controls, payment statuses, and financial operations all behave predictably.

Avion Select was RBC's expansion of Avion Rewards to people who didn't already bank with RBC.

Once we served non-RBC members, we had to revisit identity, authentication, onboarding, eligibility, and how people could actually access the rewards they'd earned.

One example was cashback. RBC banking customers already had a way to receive it into their RBC deposit accounts. Non-RBC members needed a different payout route, which is why the Interac e-Transfer withdrawal work was important to the overall proposition.

My role was owning core consumer product experiences and coordinating across identity, platform, payments, and risk partners to make those capabilities work as one journey, rather than as disconnected features. The broader Avion Select proposition grew to roughly 500,000 members.

What I found interesting was that entering a new customer segment exposed platform assumptions that had been easy to overlook when we only served the original audience. That's a useful lesson for any product expanding into new markets: you have to examine what your workflows quietly assume about the people using them.

At HBC, I worked on growth and commercial performance for a Mastercard portfolio of more than 500,000 accounts.

One thing that became clear was that acquisition wasn't the whole story. We could bring in new cardholders, but if they made their first purchase and then stopped using the card, we weren't creating much long-term value. So we looked at the journey across application, activation, repeat spending, and retention—not just the top of the funnel.

On the acquisition side, we worked with our financial-services partner, Neo, to improve the digital credit application experience. We focused on reducing friction in the application flow, while keeping the credit decisioning and required controls intact. That work improved application completion by around 15%, with decisions typically delivered in under three minutes.

Across the broader portfolio, we used cohorts and controlled experiments to make better lifecycle decisions. Over the period, active cardholders increased by four percentage points, spend per active cardholder by about 5%, and modeled customer lifetime value by roughly 10%.

What I liked about that role was the need to look beyond the obvious metric. A higher application conversion rate matters, but so do the quality of the customers you're acquiring, how they behave afterward, and whether the economics hold up. I'd approach restaurant reservations with the same discipline: more bookings are only a win if they produce real business value.

One example that comes to mind is ShopPlus at RBC Avion.

We already had a cashback offering where customers could find and activate offers through Avion. But there was a fairly fundamental point of friction: we were asking people to remember to visit a rewards platform before they went shopping.

When you think about how people actually shop online, most start with a retailer or a product they're already interested in—not by checking a rewards program first. So one hypothesis we explored was that customers weren't necessarily uninterested in cashback; we just weren't reaching them at the right moment.

We could have put more effort into reminders or better offer discovery inside Avion. But those options still depended on customers remembering to come to us first.

With ShopPlus, we took a different approach. The browser extension brought eligible cashback offers into the customer's shopping journey. When someone visited a participating retailer, they could discover and activate an offer without leaving the site.

There were technical considerations too, around recognizing merchants, activating offers, and correctly attributing qualifying purchases.

The extension reached more than 100,000 downloads. That's evidence of distribution, not proof of sustained value on its own; I'd also want to understand activations, qualifying purchases, and repeat use.

The bigger takeaway for me is that sometimes the right product decision isn't to add more to your own experience. It's to meet customers in the workflow they're already in.

We were building a program around care, repairs, trade-ins, and member benefits, but our systems were fragmented. The mobile app was also run by an external partner, so a full native integration would add substantial cost and dependencies.

I recommended starting web-first. It wasn't that mobile wasn't important; I just didn't think the full integration was needed to validate the initial proposition.

I worked with engineering and architecture to make the options clearer: what the full integration would require, what a lighter mobile presence could achieve, and how each would affect scope and timing. We landed on a more limited mobile scope rather than the full integration.

I think influencing without authority comes from being consistent about the outcome while being flexible about the approach. I try to distinguish three things: what we know, what we're assuming, and which unknowns could actually change the decision.

We moved toward a smaller web-first MVP and separated what needed the broader platform from what could happen independently. For reversible decisions, I'd rather make a call and learn. The sponsors chose limited mobile scope, and I'd have escalated the decision sooner.

questions.answer:
I try to separate recovering the customer outcome from recovering the original plan. If a dependency slips, the first question is whether we can still deliver a useful and honest subset safely.

At Arc'teryx, the membership program had many integrations and operational dependencies. That reinforced the value of phasing capabilities instead of assuming everything had to arrive at once.

I'd establish the immediate impact, options and decision owner; communicate early to partners; and set an explicit point to revisit the plan. Then I'd do a blameless review of why the dependency surprised us and what controls or sequencing changes would reduce recurrence.

I wouldn't claim a specific incident I can't verify. The principle is that preserving trust and a valid customer promise matters more than preserving a date on a slide.

Take the membership MVP at Arc'teryx. Once the dependencies became clearer, it was important to distinguish the longer-term vision from what needed to be in the first release. When time is tight, I start by making the problem and decision rights clear. At RBC, cashback withdrawals had dependencies on payments, AML, risk and financial operations, so the critical path wasn't only what the consumer team could build.

I'd identify the small number of outcomes that must hold at launch, give owners to critical dependencies, and escalate exceptions early. For a transaction flow, eligibility, status handling and reconciliation aren't optional polish.

Under pressure I prefer reducing scope to reducing reliability. I also keep the team close to the customer impact, because it's easy to optimize for the project milestone when everyone is busy.

That's relevant to restaurant product, where a problem during dinner service is immediately visible to guests and staff.

The critical distinction is that the number of tables hasn't changed, but the restaurant's ability to serve them has. I'd protect confirmed reservations where possible and give the host or manager a quick way to slow *new* demand without rebuilding the whole shift.

OpenTable already supports one-tap availability and pacing changes, so I wouldn't pitch that as a new product. The opportunity I'd explore is making the right response easier to choose: 'You're down two servers; here are the sections most at risk and a suggested pacing adjustment,' with the operator approving it.

I'd consider the kitchen, floor layout and existing guest commitments before recommending anything. If the owner refuses to restrict future bookings, I wouldn't silently override them. I'd show the expected effect on seating delays and service quality, offer lower-risk alternatives and let them make the business decision.

I'd avoid making a global launch call from a single aggregate forecast. Different markets can have very different data quality, workflows and regulations, so a model that's strong in North America may be unreliable somewhere new.

I'd establish minimum eligibility criteria by market and restaurant segment: data completeness, calibration, operator ability to override, customer support readiness and the value of the recommendation against an existing rules baseline.

I'd roll out to segments that meet those thresholds, with monitoring and a way to turn recommendations off quickly. For markets that don't, I'd keep the proven manual or rules-based experience rather than pretend the AI is ready everywhere.

I'd tell leadership the expansion path and what we must learn to unlock the next markets. 'Global' should mean consistent trust, not identical functionality on day one.

questions.answer:
I'd separate what should be consistent globally from what needs to adapt to local restaurant behavior. The basics — a reservation, party size, table, availability and service status — should live on a common platform.

But how restaurants use those concepts varies. Some markets lean more heavily on walk-ins or local reservation services. Some have different expectations around deposits, dining duration, language and guest communication. POS integration can vary as well.

I'd learn those workflows from operators in the market before writing requirements, then prefer configuration and extension points over country-specific forks. I'd validate the product with a few representative restaurants, including a busy service, before scaling.

The measures I'd care about are onboarding time, booking and seating reliability, use during actual service, and retention. A translated app with low operator adoption isn't a successful market launch.

I'd map the actual shift: bookings arriving, guests checking in, walk-ins, seating, table status, late parties and last-minute problems. Then I'd look for steps where the host has to leave the floor, re-enter information or make a risky adjustment under time pressure.

I'd favor quick, reversible actions, clear statuses and the ability to override automation. If a server calls in sick, the most useful product might be a reliable way to adjust future pacing without disturbing confirmed guests.

I'd validate with real operators during service and measure time to complete critical tasks, errors and overrides, not just clicks.

An independent restaurant might need the essential reservation and floor workflows to be reliable and easy to set up. I'd view market expansion as a sequence of operational proofs, not just a country launch date.

First, can we onboard the restaurant and represent its floor and booking rules correctly? Second, can it run a real lunch or dinner service without breakdowns? Third, do the operator and diners have a good enough experience to use it again?

I'd instrument that journey with time to first live shift, reservations handled successfully, seating issues, urgent support contacts and retention. I'd also want local qualitative feedback, because a metric can miss a subtle workflow mismatch.

I'd start with a small group across different venue types and only scale once the failure modes are understood. I'd rather learn that a particular integration or guest expectation needs work in ten restaurants than across a whole new market.

I'd push back on a global launch if the evidence says some restaurants can't use the feature reliably. The way I'd frame it to leadership is not 'the team isn't ready,' but 'here's the business risk and a safer path to the same outcome.'

Suppose the AI recommends pacing adjustments that work well in urban North American restaurants but poorly in smaller venues abroad. I'd show the segment-level quality and operator feedback, then recommend launching where it clears an agreed bar while keeping a proven rules-based experience elsewhere.

That gives us a credible launch and a plan to expand, rather than an arbitrary all-or-nothing argument. I'd be explicit about the trade-off: we sacrifice some initial reach to protect operator trust and avoid service disruptions.

If leadership wants to proceed anyway, I'd make the decision rights, guardrails and rollback plan very clear.
